metadata.title: ACKS Core Construction Rules Summary
metadata.design_goal: This summary preserves mechanics, procedures, definitions, and tables in a structure suitable for later translation into executable systems.

style_rules.rule: Flavor text, examples, and non-mechanical prose omitted.
Sections are organized as definitions, inputs, procedures, outputs, constraints, and tables.
Where a source table appears textually corrupted in the uploaded markdown, values are preserved conservatively rather than invented.

shared_concepts.definition: The judge constructs settings, regions, cities, dungeons, and encounter distributions.
A 24-mile hex map used for the broad campaign area.
A 6-mile hex map used for the starting region.
A basic territorial unit used by ACKS domain mechanics.
A political aggregation of domains, ranging from barony to empire.
A settlement market size category used for trade range and starting-city generation.
A per-merchandise economic modifier for a market, generated by base rolls plus adjustments.
A static location on a regional map such as a settlement, castle, dungeon, lair, or special area.
A monster habitation that may include treasure and multiple encounter groups.
A special room, area, or encounter whose function is not a standard monster/trap/empty result.

inputs.input: One campaign map at 24-mile hex scale.
One regional map at 6-mile hex scale.

procedure.step: Create a campaign map on 24-mile hexes.
Create a regional map on 6-mile hexes.
Decide shorelines, landmasses, climate, and terrain before final placement.
Record mountains, rivers, lakes, seas, and other features that create trade routes or barriers.
Choose or infer realm sizes and populations from maps or source material.
Use the realm type tables to determine population, domains, and area.
Optionally decompose larger realms into vassal realms using the political divisions table.
Use the revenue table to estimate holdings and incomes of rulers and vassals.
For a default world, assume about 50 people per square mile, equivalent to 300 families per 6-mile hex and 5,000 families per 24-mile hex.

constraints.rule: On the recommended two-map setup, the 24-mile campaign map should cover a very large realm or several kingdoms.
On the recommended two-map setup, the 6-mile regional map should represent a strong principality with about 50% of the map left unsettled wilderness.

procedure.step: Start from the default assumption of 50 people per square mile.
Increase realm size if using a lower-density world.
Decrease realm size if using a higher-density world.

constraints.rule: Unsettled hexes with no settled inhabitants and no garrison do not count toward size or population density for this purpose.

definitions.definition: ACKS assumes about 10% of a realm's population lives in urban communities.
ACKS assumes about 20% of the urban population lives in the largest settlement.

procedure.step: Determine realm or domain population in families.
Consult the villages/towns/cities placement table to determine urban population, largest settlement size, monthly urban income, and market class.
If the realm contains vassal realms, determine the largest settlement for each vassal realm and place it within that realm.
Place urban settlements preferentially on rivers, lakes, coastlines, and roads.
Treat remaining population as living in isolated homesteads and hamlets after the major urban settlements are placed.

constraints.rule: Class IV and smaller settlements can be ignored on the 24-mile campaign map.
Class VI settlements can be ignored on the 6-mile regional map.
Monthly revenue of urban settlements is already factored into the revenue-by-realm-type values.

definitions.definition: Demand modifiers can be assigned by discretion or generated mechanically.
These rules also apply to adventurer domains.

procedure.step: For each merchandise type, roll 1d3-1d3 to generate a base demand modifier from -2 to +2.
Apply all relevant environmental adjustments for age, water source, climate, and elevation.
After applying environmental modifiers, drop any fractions.
Apply domain land-revenue adjustments by assigning positive and negative modifiers to the indicated number of merchandise types.
Apply racial production adjustments if the market is associated with the listed race.
If markets are connected by a valid trade route, shift demand modifiers toward one another as specified by market sizes.

row.cell: +1 to 6 merchandise types; -1 to 1 merchandise type
+1 to 4 merchandise types; -1 to 1 merchandise type
+1 to 2 merchandise types; -1 to 1 merchandise type
+1 to 1 merchandise type; -1 to 1 merchandise type
-1 to 2 merchandise types; +1 to 1 merchandise type
-1 to 4 merchandise types; +1 to 1 merchandise type
-1 to 6 merchandise types; +1 to 1 merchandise type
-2 to beer/ale, common metals, tools, armor/weapons, rare metals, semi-precious stones, and gems
-2 to common wood, dyes/pigments, cloth, glassware, and porcelain

trade_route_rules.rule: Two criteria are required for a trade route: a connecting road/trail/navigable waterway, and both markets must lie within each other's trade range.
If connected markets are different sizes, shift all demand modifiers of the smaller market 2 points toward the larger market, or set them equal if the difference is less than 2.
If connected markets are equal size, each shifts each demand modifier 1 point toward the other.
When processing a region, begin with the largest market and work outward through direct trade routes, then continue to the next markets.

procedure.step: Determine appropriate high-level NPC rulers for the highest-tier realms in the campaign setting.
Determine rulers for the largest realms, cities, and towns on the regional map.
Use level frequency and maximum NPC population tables to estimate plausible numbers of leveled characters.

constraints.rule: It is not necessary to pre-assign every domain an NPC ruler or calculate every NPC location in advance.

procedure.step: Build the 6-mile regional map.
Place around 45 static points of interest.
Allocate roughly one-third of points to settlements, towns, and castles.
Allocate roughly two-thirds of points to dungeons, lairs, and special areas.
Of the 30 dungeons, include about 3 large dungeons for 6-10 sessions, 10 dungeons for 1-2 sessions, and 17 small lairs for a half-session or 1-3 encounters.
Write one paragraph of description for each point of interest initially.
Fully detail the small lairs; leave larger dungeons brief for later development.

definitions.definition: Static points of interest exist at a density of about one per 6 hexes, or 36 miles.
Dynamic lairs are additional mobile or seasonal monster presences beyond the static points.

procedure.step: Use the maximum NPC population table as a plausibility benchmark for numbers of leveled rulers and notable NPCs in realms.
Populate the region with wilderness movement, lairs, and changing threats appropriate to the map's density and civilization frontier.
Design the regional map as a borderlands structure.
Place a string of border forts, towns, or other settlements along one axis of the map, about halfway in.
Place the region's largest town or settlement behind the border forts.
Place most wilderness dungeons and lairs beyond the border forts.
Increase danger the deeper the party travels into the wilderness.
Optionally place a few unusually dangerous but geographically isolated areas near the border.
Place one low-level mega-dungeon near the border, one mid-level mega-dungeon at moderate distance, and one extremely hard mega-dungeon on the far side of the map.
Build dynamic lairs and wandering encounters at a mid-range difficulty of about 5th-9th level.

design_effects.effect: Low-level parties tend to travel between border settlements, clearing nearby threats.
Mid-level parties begin entering the wilderness and exploring outward in widening circles.
High-level parties conduct deep wilderness forays and often begin founding or seizing strongholds.

procedure.step: Choose one settlement on the regional map as the starting city.
Prefer a border town with a low-level dungeon nearby.
Use previously determined population, demand modifiers, and ruler.
Flesh out the city with named authority, churches, thieves' guild, and militia sized to the settlement.
Use the starting cities table to determine minimum ruler level, market class, and approximate local numbers of leveled NPCs by class.

definitions.definition: Total membership is the total number of criminals in the city's guild structure for the given market class.
Highest boss level is the expected level of the most powerful boss in the city.
Monthly syndicate revenue is the revenue generated by the boss's syndicate in that city.
Monthly guild revenue is the wider guild revenue including syndicates in other settlements.

membership_distribution.rule: 35% are 1st level characters of appropriate criminal classes.

procedure.step: Use market class to determine total membership, boss level, and revenues.
If the settlement is part of a larger realm, use the parenthetical boss level value.
Optionally divide criminals into multiple competing or complementary guilds instead of one unified guild.
If split into multiple guilds, base boss level and revenues on the membership of each separate guild rather than settlement market class.

definitions.definition: The starting city can be used to deliver rumors, legends, clues, and motivations for dungeon and wilderness exploration.

section.implementation_note: Mechanical content in this section is primarily the reuse of the starting-city and criminal-guild frameworks above as infrastructure for scenario generation.

procedure.step: Choose the dungeon type.
Draw the dungeon map.
Stock each room.
Place monsters.
Place traps.
Add unique encounters.
Assign treasure.
Finalize room descriptions and track future changes.
Choose or roll the dungeon type on 1d20.
Draw the map on square graph paper.
Shape the map to fit the dungeon type.
Roll once on the dungeon stocking table for each room on each dungeon level.
Record results separately by dungeon level.
Assign each result to a specific room in a way that fits dungeon logic and entertainment value.
For each monster result, choose or roll a monster encounter appropriate to the dungeon level.
Roll on the dungeon wandering monster level table to determine which monster-level table to consult.
Use the random monsters by level table to determine monster type and number appearing.
Assign encounters to rooms based on level relationships, chokepoints, access to stairs, and monster logic.
Consult the monster entry to determine whether the encounter is in lair.
For ordinary monsters, check % In Lair where applicable.
If monsters are in lair, treasure is present according to later treasure rules.
If the stocking process produced multiple encounters of an organized monster type, assume the dungeon contains a lair of that type.
Choose one room as the lair and place the other rolled groups nearby as guard posts, barracks, splinter colonies, or similar support areas.
Add leaders, champions, females, young, and other associated creatures indicated by the monster entry.
If only one organized group is rolled and that monster's lair size can exceed one group, either treat it as a small lair, add more groups to complete a lair, or treat it as an isolated group.

placement_rules.rule: Lower-level monsters can be placed near inter-level connections or as guards for stronger intelligent monsters.
Higher-level intelligent monsters can be placed in hidden or inaccessible areas.
Powerful unintelligent monsters may dominate isolated sub-areas alone.

definitions.definition: Traps are obstacles intended to harm, capture, delay, separate, or alarm dungeon explorers.

procedure.step: Place traps with a purpose, such as area protection, passage interdiction, or alarm-raising.
Define each trap's trigger.
Whenever an adventurer takes an action that could trigger a trap, roll 1d6.
On 1-2, the trap springs.
Resolve the trap's effect, including any attack throw or saving throw specified by the trap.

trap.effect: An arrow attacks one adventurer as a 1st level fighter for 1d6+1 damage.
Each adventurer in a 10-foot radius saves versus Blast or suffers 2d6 damage.
A pit opens beneath all adventurers in a 10-foot by 10-foot square.
trap.depth_rule: Pits should generally be 10 feet deep per dungeon level.

trap.effect: A dart attacks one adventurer as a 1st level fighter for 1d4+1 damage.
trap.secondary_effect: If hit, the target must save versus Poison or die.

trap.effect: The adventurer who triggered the trap must save versus Poison or die.
The triggering adventurer saves versus Blast or suffers 3d6 damage.
trap.secondary_effect: The way is blocked and the party may be separated.

trap.effect: All adventurers in the room or hallway save versus Blast or suffer 2d6 damage.
All adventurers in a 10-foot line save versus Blast or suffer 1d8 damage.
As camouflaged pit trap, plus the falling adventurer lands on 1d4 spikes.
trap.spike_damage: Each spike deals 1d6 damage in addition to falling damage.

definitions.definition: Unique encounters are special rooms or areas distinguished from ordinary empty, monster, or trap rooms.

procedure.step: Design unique encounters deliberately rather than randomly.
Consider how dungeon inhabitants know about, exploit, or avoid the feature.
Optionally attach monsters suited to puzzles, guardianship, deception, or magical service.

row.cell: Green slime, wood golem, yellow mold
Gelatinous cube, gray ooze, animated statue (iron, crystal), doppelganger, shadow
Animated statue (stone), ochre jelly, rust monster
Golem (amber, bronze), black pudding, djinni, efreeti, elemental

procedure.step: After monsters, traps, and unique features are placed, assign treasure to rooms.
Monster lairs have treasure according to the monster's treasure type.
Empty rooms have treasure 15% of the time.
Trap rooms have treasure 30% of the time.
For treasure in empty or trap rooms, determine treasure type using the unprotected treasure table by dungeon level and 1d6.
Place lair treasure in forms that make sense for the monster.
Usually hide unprotected treasure rather than leave it openly visible.
In trapped rooms, treasure can be hidden or be on previous victims.
Place treasure in unique rooms as needed, especially to support level wealth targets or to entice interaction with the feature.
Sum treasure on the level and compare it to total monster XP available.
Target an ideal ratio of 4 gp of treasure per 1 XP from monsters.
If treasure is too low, remove some monsters or add treasure.
If treasure is too high, add monsters or reduce treasure.
Add room and passage descriptions sufficient for play.
Fully describe only a minority of rooms if desired, especially rooms with special or unique encounters.
Keep improvised significant details written down for continuity.
For multi-level dungeons used repeatedly, treat the dungeon as a living place that changes in response to player action and resident monster behavior.
